name: Myasthenia Gravis

ethnicAssociations: Male predominance or equal in late-onset (>50 years)

criteria.description: Fluctuating weakness of voluntary muscles that worsens with activity and improves with rest
Decremental response (>10%) on repetitive nerve stimulation at 2-3 Hz
Positive response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (edrophonium/ice pack test)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Clinical picture of fatigable weakness plus at least one confirmatory test (antibodies, RNS, or SFEMG)
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Seronegative MG (~10-15%) lacks AChR and MuSK antibodies but has compatible clinical and electrophysiological findings. LRP4 antibodies may be present in some seronegative patients.

pathognomonic.notes: Worsens with sustained upgaze; most common presenting sign
Fluctuating and variable; does not conform to single nerve palsy pattern

pathognomonic.symptomName: Fatigable weakness worsening with repetitive use
pathognomonic.notes: Cardinal feature: weakness worsens with activity, improves with rest

common.notes: Nasal speech, difficulty chewing, liquids may come out of nose
Voice becomes progressively weaker during conversation

occasional.notes: Dyspnea on exertion; can progress to myasthenic crisis
Jaw may hang open after prolonged chewing

rare.symptomName: Isolated limb weakness without ocular symptoms
rare.notes: Uncommon presentation; usually ocular symptoms develop
Life-threatening; requires ICU admission and ventilatory support

laboratory: AChR (acetylcholine receptor) antibodies positive in ~85% of generalized MG
MuSK antibodies positive in ~5-8% of generalized MG
LRP4 antibodies in some seronegative patients
Anti-striated muscle (titin) antibodies associated with thymoma
imaging: CT or MRI chest to evaluate for thymoma (present in ~10-15%)
Thymic hyperplasia common in early-onset AChR-positive MG
genetic: HLA-B8, DR3 association with early-onset MG
Congenital myasthenic syndromes have distinct genetic causes (not autoimmune)
other: Repetitive nerve stimulation showing >10% decremental response at 2-3 Hz
Single-fiber EMG showing increased jitter (most sensitive test, >95%)
Ice pack test: improvement of ptosis with ice application for 2 minutes
Forced vital capacity monitoring for respiratory involvement

distinguishingFeatures: ALS has upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia)
ALS weakness is progressive, not fluctuating
ALS does not affect ocular muscles
ALS has EMG showing denervation, not NMJ dysfunction
GBS has ascending weakness, typically monophasic
GBS has albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF
GBS does not have fatigable weakness pattern
IBM has distal finger flexor and quadriceps weakness
IBM weakness is progressive, not fatigable
IBM has characteristic muscle biopsy findings

redFlags: Acute respiratory decompensation (myasthenic crisis) is a medical emergency
New onset or worsening weakness after starting aminoglycosides, beta-blockers, or magnesium
Thymoma must be excluded with chest imaging in all MG patients
MuSK-positive MG may not respond to pyridostigmine and can worsen
Rapid deterioration after recent infection or surgery
Negative AChR and MuSK antibodies should prompt consideration of congenital myasthenic syndromes in young patients
references: Gilhus NE, et al. Myasthenia gravis. Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2019;5(1):30.
Sanders DB, et al. International consensus guidance for management of myasthenia gravis. Neurology. 2016;87(4):419-425.
Dresser L, et al. Myasthenia Gravis: Epidemiology, Pathophysiology and Clinical Manifestations. J Clin Med. 2021;10(11):2235.
